clai_00001.text: The modified convolution function reduces the mean absolute error for formation‑energy prediction from 0.112 eV/atom to 0.039 eV/atom, achieving DFT‑level accuracy comparable to the experimental DFT‑experiment error of 0.081–0.136 eV/atom.

clai_00002.text: CGCNN classifies metals versus semiconductors with an area under the ROC curve of 0.95 and an overall accuracy of 0.90.

clai_00003.text: By extracting per‑atom site energies in perovskites, the model reveals that large‑radius elements stabilize the A site and group 4‑6 elements stabilize the B site, and using these insights the high‑throughput search space for stable perovskites is reduced by a factor of seven (from 18,928 to 228 candidates).

clai_00004.text: When applied to a set of 1,585 crystals with elastic properties, CGCNN predicts bulk modulus with a mean absolute error of 0.077 log(GPa) and shear modulus with a mean absolute error of 0.114 log(GPa), demonstrating good generalization.

clai_00005.text: Using roughly 10⁴ training examples, CGCNN attains DFT‑level accuracy for eight distinct material properties across diverse crystal types and compositions.

clai_00006.text: Compared with a prior statistical‑learning approach, CGCNN achieves similar or lower root‑mean‑square errors for bulk modulus (0.075 log(GPa) vs 0.105) and shear modulus (0.127 log(GPa) vs 0.138) using the same training data.

clai_00007.text: Representing crystals as graphs of atoms and bonds provides a universal, size‑invariant input format applicable to any periodic crystal system.

clai_00008.text: The Materials Project database contains computed structural, electronic, and energetic data for over 33,000 inorganic compounds, generated using more than 15 million CPU‑hours of computation.

clai_00009.text: The Materials Project provides an open RESTful API and a high‑level Python library (pymatgen) that enable programmatic querying and analysis of the full dataset.

clai_00010.text: The workflow software FireWorks together with the custodian job‑management tool automatically manages high‑throughput DFT calculations, self‑heals failed runs, and applies material‑type‑specific workflows.

clai_00011.text: Visual warnings are displayed on the Materials Project website for compounds whose calculated oxidation states, cell volumes, or bond lengths deviate significantly from experimental norms, helping users assess data reliability.

clai_00012.text: Automated validation checks compare calculated oxidation states, cell volumes, and bond lengths against experimental data and flag outliers for user review.

clai_00013.text: Using Materials Project tools, researchers designed a new class of sodium‑based carbonophosphate compounds, predicted them to be thermodynamically stable, synthesized them hydrothermally, and experimentally confirmed their Li‑ion battery performance after ion exchange.

clai_00014.text: High‑throughput computational screening through the Materials Project has screened tens of thousands of compounds and identified promising candidates for solar water splitting, photovoltaics, topological insulators, scintillators, CO₂ capture, piezoelectrics, thermoelectrics, catalysis, hydrogen storage, and Li‑ion batteries, with experimental hits reported in several areas.

clai_00015.text: The Materials Project aims to reduce the typical 10–20 year timeline for advanced material development by providing large‑scale accurate information, thereby accelerating discovery for clean energy, electronics, and other sectors.

clai_00016.text: The distribution of chromium coordination environments in oxides derived from the database matches known chemical principles: Cr⁶⁺ prefers tetrahedral (4‑fold) coordination, while Cr³⁺ prefers octahedral (6‑fold) coordination.

clai_00017.text: The Materials Project website receives several hundred unique page views per day and has registered over 4,000 users from academia, government, and industry.

clai_00018.text: Class‑specific computational methodologies and reference reactions are applied for solid‑gas, d‑block oxide, and dissolved‑ion systems to improve agreement with experimental data.

clai_00019.text: The open‑source software infrastructure of the Materials Project, including pymatgen, has attracted more than 100 active collaborators worldwide and incorporates community contributions such as FEFF and ABINIT support.

clai_00020.text: Future development plans include adding calculations of surface energies, elastic constants, point defects, finite‑temperature properties, and implementing a two‑way ‘calculations‑on‑demand’ feature for user‑submitted compounds.

clai_00021.text: The ConvLSTM model accurately predicts fracture patterns, crack‑length trends, and both mode‑I (tensile) and mode‑II (shear) loading responses across crystal orientations, closely matching atomistic molecular dynamics simulations, with only a minor discrepancy for the x100 orientation under mode‑II shear.

clai_00022.text: The model predicts fracture toughness values that are comparable to those obtained from atomistic molecular dynamics simulations.

clai_00023.text: A model trained exclusively on single‑crystal data generalizes to bicrystal and gradient‑orientation crystals, reproducing MD fracture patterns for small orientation differences, capturing overall crack paths for large orientation differences, and handling arbitrary geometry gradients.

clai_00024.text: The ConvLSTM approach reduces computational cost dramatically compared with full molecular dynamics simulations, enabling rapid fracture predictions.

clai_00025.text: Representing molecular dynamics results as image‑based geometric matrices preserves crystal orientation information and allows the neural network to learn spatiotemporal fracture behavior.

clai_00026.text: The training dataset comprises 14,300 paired geometric‑crack image matrices, and the model exhibits convergent loss during training.

clai_00027.text: JARVIS-DFT contains approximately 40,000 materials and about 1 million calculated properties.

clai_00028.text: The integrated JARVIS workflow (DFT → FF → ML) enables rapid screening of materials for high solar‑cell efficiency (SLME) with predictions validated against experimental data.

clai_00029.text: Machine‑learning models trained on Classical Force‑field Inspired Descriptors (CFID) achieve high predictive accuracy for formation energies, exfoliation energies, band gaps, magnetic moments, refractive indices, dielectric constants, thermoelectric performance, and piezoelectric/infrared modes.

clai_00030.text: Using the vdW‑DF‑OptB88 functional for all dimensionalities yields accurate lattice parameters and formation energies for both van‑der‑Waals and non‑vdW bonded materials.

clai_00031.text: The meta‑GGA TBmBJ potential predicts band gaps with accuracy comparable to the hybrid HSE06 functional while requiring up to ten times less computational effort.

clai_00032.text: Comparisons of JARVIS‑DFT computed formation energies, band gaps, and elastic constants with experimental measurements show acceptable error margins, confirming the database’s predictive reliability.

clai_00033.text: Beyond‑DFT methods (HSE06, PBE0, G0W0, DMFT) are generated for a subset of materials to provide higher‑level reference data and enable uncertainty quantification.

clai_00034.text: JARVIS‑FF includes data for roughly 1,500 materials and about 110 classical force‑fields.

clai_00035.text: JARVIS‑ML provides around 25 machine‑learning models for predicting material properties.

clai_00036.text: JARVIS‑Tools implements automatic k‑point convergence protocols that improve the precision of DFT calculations.

clai_00037.text: JARVIS‑FF automatically computes bulk modulus, defect formation energies, and phonon spectra for each force‑field and compares them with DFT results to assess force‑field quality.

clai_00038.text: A REST‑API is provided for programmatic download and upload of JARVIS data, supporting community contributions and interoperability.

clai_00039.text: Interpretability analyses of JARVIS‑ML models reveal physical insights that go beyond conventional materials‑science intuition.

clai_00040.text: LiFlow predicts lithium mean‑squared displacement with a Spearman rank correlation of 0.7–0.8 on unseen material compositions, enabling screening of high‑diffusivity electrolytes.

clai_00041.text: LiFlow achieves speed‑ups of up to ~600,000× over ab initio molecular dynamics (and ~400× over MLIP), predicting a 1 ns trajectory in 48 s for a 2 × 2 × 1 LGPS supercell and 352 s for a 4 × 4 × 4 supercell.

clai_00042.text: The computational cost of LiFlow scales linearly with the number of atoms (O(n)), in contrast to the cubic scaling (O(n³)) of ab initio molecular dynamics.

clai_00043.text: Incorporating an adaptive, thermally and chemically conditioned Maxwell–Boltzmann prior markedly lowers mean absolute errors and raises rank correlations for MSD and RDF compared with an isotropic prior; ablation studies show performance degradation without it.

clai_00044.text: Incorporating the Corrector model reduces RDF mean absolute error and mitigates large‑displacement artifacts, improving MSD prediction across temperatures, especially for hydrogen diffusion.

clai_00045.text: LiFlow trained on 25 ps ab initio molecular dynamics trajectories can generate stable trajectories up to 1 ns in larger (4 × 4 × 4) supercells, reproducing lithium self‑diffusivity, activation energies, and temperature dependence comparable to long AIMD simulations.

clai_00046.text: Within the training temperature range, LiFlow’s predicted diffusivity D* closely matches reference values from Winter and Gómez‑Bombarelli.

clai_00047.text: A direct regression (Regressor) model yields higher mean‑squared‑displacement errors than the generative LiFlow model, demonstrating the necessity of generative modeling for accurate atomic transport simulation.

clai_00048.text: When extrapolating to temperatures lower than the training range, LiFlow’s predicted diffusivity D* decreases more slowly than reference data, indicating fictitious diffusive behavior at high 1000/T.

clai_00049.text: The adaptive prior classifier provides limited benefit at the lowest temperature (600 K), reducing its overall effectiveness under that condition.

clai_00050.text: LiFlow qualitatively captures ion transport behavior in sodium‑based conductors despite being trained only on lithium‑containing materials.

clai_00051.text: LiFlow reproduces structural features such as diffusion traces, probability densities, and potentials of mean force for lithium; accuracy is high at lower temperatures with only slight deviations at higher temperatures.

clai_00052.text: A curated dataset of 476 binary ionic compound melting temperatures spanning 0-4,000°C was compiled for machine learning model development.

clai_00053.text: The best one-step gradient-boosted tree regression model achieves 165±4 K MAE and 0.89 R² on the test set for melting temperature prediction.

clai_00054.text: A two-step approach combining unsupervised clustering with supervised regression achieves 156±4 K MAE and 0.92 R², outperforming direct one-step supervised learning.

clai_00055.text: Cluster 1 (198 compounds, mostly ionic halides and oxides) achieves 136±5 K MAE and 0.92 R², while Cluster 2 (222 compounds, mostly covalent carbides and nitrides) achieves 189±7 K MAE and 0.90 R².

clai_00056.text: Cohesive energy and elastic moduli (shear and bulk modulus) are the most important features for melting temperature prediction, as identified by both ensemble feature importance and SHAP analysis.

clai_00057.text: Models trained without elastic moduli features yield errors greater than 400 K, demonstrating that elastic features are necessary for accurate melting temperature predictions.

clai_00058.text: Very-high melting temperatures (>3150 K) appear only in Cluster 2, predominantly in metal carbides, reflecting the covalent bonding character of these materials.

clai_00059.text: Tree ensemble methods (gradient-boosted trees and random forest regression) substantially outperform linear models, which achieve MAE >240 K and RMSE >340 K, at least 100 K worse than non-linear approaches.

clai_00060.text: The two-step clustering approach provides interpretability by revealing different melting physics dominated by bonding types, with Cluster 1 governed by ionic bonding features and Cluster 2 by covalent bonding features.

clai_00061.text: VS-SISSO symbolic regression generates interpretable expressions for melting temperature that provide qualitative insight into the melting physics dominating within each cluster.

clai_00062.text: Cluster 2 melting temperatures can be accurately represented with symbolic models depending on only two features: squared cohesive energy and inverse square root of periodic groups or electronegativities.

clai_00063.text: Symbolic regression results corroborate that cohesive energy and elastic moduli are the most important features, consistent with feature importance and SHAP analysis from tree ensemble models.

clai_00064.text: The featurization methods are transferable to more complex compositions, enabling new ML models to be fitted without revising the materials embedding method given extended datasets.

clai_00065.text: CHGNet achieves state-of-the-art performance on the Matbench Discovery benchmark, outperforming eight other submitted models.

clai_00066.text: On the Materials Project Trajectory test set, CHGNet trained with magnetic moment labels attains mean absolute errors of 30 meV/atom for energy, 77 meV/Å for forces, 0.348 GPa for stress, and 0.032 µB for magnetic moments.

clai_00067.text: CHGNet molecular dynamics simulations of Li superionic conductors reproduce room‑temperature ionic conductivities and activation energies within the error bars of AIMD, correctly distinguishing faster from slower conductors.

clai_00068.text: CHGNet integrates magnetic moment labels as a proxy for atomic charge, enabling inference of atomic charges and accurate differentiation of oxidation states such as V³⁺/V⁴⁺ and Fe²⁺/Fe³⁺.

clai_00069.text: In charge‑informed molecular dynamics of Li₀.₅MnO₂ at 1100 K, CHGNet predicts the emergence of Mn²⁺ after ~0.8 ns, coinciding with a ~50 meV/oxygen reduction in potential energy and the formation of a spinel‑like phase, indicating a correlation between charge disproportionation and phase transformation.

clai_00070.text: Including electronic entropy via charge‑decorated cluster expansions, CHGNet reproduces the experimentally observed miscibility gap and eutectoid‑like transition in the LiₓFePO₄ phase diagram, whereas a non‑charge‑decorated model fails to capture these features.

clai_00071.text: CHGNet accurately predicts the dramatic increase in Li‑ion diffusivity and the reduction of activation energy (~160 meV) in slightly Li‑stuffed Li₃La₃Te₂O₁₂, matching DFT‑computed values and the activated diffusion network theory.

clai_00072.text: Fine‑tuning the pretrained CHGNet on the Li‑Fe‑P‑O chemical space reduces the test error from 23 meV/atom to 15 meV/atom.

clai_00073.text: CHGNet captures long‑range interactions up to 20 Å with only four atom‑convolution layers while maintaining low computational cost.

clai_00074.text: CHGNet enables nanosecond‑scale molecular dynamics simulations of garnet Li₃La₃Te₂O₁₂, yielding lithium self‑diffusion coefficients with quantified uncertainty.

clai_00075.text: Using magnetic moments as a charge proxy does not strictly ensure global charge neutrality in CHGNet predictions.

clai_00076.text: The Materials Project Trajectory dataset used to pre‑train CHGNet contains approximately 1.58 million atomic configurations spanning 94 elements, with magnetic moment labels for 76 elements, providing comprehensive chemical coverage.

clai_00077.text: After fine‑tuning, CHGNet serves as a data‑efficient model for high‑precision simulations across diverse chemistries, supporting high‑throughput screening efforts.

clai_00078.text: Continuous-filter convolutional (cfconv) layers enable convolution on arbitrarily positioned inputs, overcoming the limitations of discrete filters that require grid-aligned data.

clai_00079.text: SchNet provides rotationally invariant energy predictions and rotationally equivariant, energy‑conserving force predictions by defining forces as the negative gradient of the predicted energy.

clai_00080.text: When trained on MD17 trajectories with a combined energy‑and‑force loss, SchNet achieves energy MAE ≤0.12 kcal/mol and force MAE ≤0.33 kcal/mol/Å, matching or surpassing GDML and DTNN on all tested molecules, including flexible ones such as malonaldehyde and ethanol.

clai_00081.text: Training SchNet with forces on only 1,000 examples yields better accuracy than training on 50,000 examples using energies alone, demonstrating that force information improves data efficiency.

clai_00082.text: On the ISO17 benchmark, SchNet reaches chemical‑accuracy (≈0.5 kcal/mol MAE) for energy predictions on molecules seen during training and further improves predictions on unseen isomers when forces are included in training.

clai_00083.text: Including force information in the training loss causally improves SchNet’s generalization to previously unseen chemical structures in ISO17.

clai_00084.text: GDML cannot be trained on 50,000 MD17 examples due to its quadratic scaling with the number of atoms and samples, whereas SchNet scales to that dataset size.

clai_00085.text: The ISO17 benchmark, comprising 645,000 conformations of 129 C7O2H10 isomers, is introduced to evaluate models on combined chemical and conformational variation.

clai_00086.text: Using a shifted softplus activation guarantees an infinitely differentiable (smooth) potential energy surface, facilitating geometry optimization.

clai_00087.text: Continuous-filter convolutions produce smoother energy predictions than discrete filters, as illustrated in Figure 1.

clai_00088.text: On the QM9 benchmark, SchNet attains a mean absolute error of 0.31 kcal/mol for total‑energy prediction with 110 k training examples, outperforming DTNN (0.84) and enn‑s2s (0.45).

clai_00089.text: Unconstrained machine-learned interatomic potentials (MLIPs) trained on large datasets achieve accuracies on par with state-of-the-art equivariant architectures while maintaining orders-of-magnitude lower computational cost than quantum-mechanical methods.

clai_00090.text: The PET model achieves state-of-the-art accuracy on matbench-discovery benchmark (DAF=6.075, Accuracy=0.977, F1=0.924) and exceeds SOTA on SPICE molecular benchmark across most subsets for both energy and force predictions.

clai_00091.text: PET-OMAD demonstrates the best overall accuracy in predicting energies and forces on MADBench in almost all cases, with the highest success rate (98.43%) in predicting desorption reactions.

clai_00092.text: Fine-tuning models pre-trained on OMat24 to the MAD dataset achieves near-converged validation metrics in 30-100 epochs versus 700+ epochs when training from scratch, halving validation energy and force errors and achieving 50% lower test error than training on MAD alone.

clai_00093.text: Non-conservative (unconstrained) MLIP models consistently show 2-3× theoretical speed-up over their conservative counterparts, with direct force prediction providing additional 2-3× speedup compared to forces computed via automatic differentiation.

clai_00094.text: The PET architecture scales to 730M parameters (OMat-XL) while maintaining tractable memory usage and computational efficiency due to increased node representation size and unconstrained architecture.

clai_00095.text: Conservative PET-OAM models achieve state-of-the-art performance on phonon tasks in matbench-discovery and the best overall accuracy in predicting shear modulus among tested models.

clai_00096.text: Non-conservative models allow residual asymmetries to drive relaxation toward more stable close-packed structures, unlike equivariant models that remain trapped in symmetric but unstable configurations, though 70% (16%) of final configurations retain symmetry of initial structure with 0.01 Å threshold for conservative (non-conservative) models.

clai_00097.text: Elastic moduli predictions are very sensitive to the lack of energy conservation in MLIP models, and non-conservative models consistently perform worse on matbench-discovery downstream tasks despite achieving better training and validation accuracies.

clai_00098.text: Central finite differences can more than halve the error for non-equivariant models on phonon calculations by averaging out inconsistencies between symmetry-equivalent displacements, and O(3)-averaging increases symmetric structures to 77% with symprec 0.01 Å in the non-conservative case.

clai_00099.text: Accurate conservative, rotationally unconstrained models can be used safely for phonon calculations, though it is recommended to use looser convergence tolerances or enforce rotational averaging when performing free geometry optimizations with unconstrained models, especially with direct-force predictions.

clai_00100.text: DFT setting inconsistency between training and evaluation datasets significantly affects MLIP model performance comparisons, with PET-OMAD performing worse than PET-OAM and PET-MPtrj on Inorganic Materials due to differences in ab initio theory levels.

clai_00101.text: The adaptive cutoff method ensures computational and parameter budget is allocated more uniformly across different structures by including a roughly-constant number of neighbors, with edge weighting by the mean of corresponding two node weights ensuring symmetry.

clai_00102.text: The PET-OMat model series spans a broad range of cost/accuracy tradeoff scenarios from 4.5M to 730M parameters, with pre-trained models released covering diverse chemical systems across the full periodic table.

clai_00103.text: Universal MLIPs trained on massive datasets can generalize across diverse chemical systems and can be successfully applied to structural optimization and lattice dynamics workflows.

clai_00104.text: UMLIPs trained on the MatPES dataset achieve test mean absolute errors in energies that are 4–10 times lower than UMLIPs trained on the larger MPRelax or OMat24 datasets.

clai_00105.text: Across equilibrium, near‑equilibrium, and molecular‑dynamics property benchmarks, MatPES‑trained UMLIPs match or surpass the performance of models trained on much larger datasets such as OMat24 (≈100 M structures).

clai_00106.text: Molecular‑dynamics simulations using MatPES‑trained UMLIPs exhibit markedly higher stability, with median termination temperatures up to ~1,900 K, versus ~1,300–1,500 K for MPRelax and OMat24 models.

clai_00107.text: On near‑equilibrium benchmarks, MatPES UMLIPs significantly improve the prediction of shear modulus (G_VRH) and off‑equilibrium forces while achieving similar bulk‑modulus (K_VRH) and heat‑capacity (C_V) accuracy compared to MPRelax and OMat24 models.

clai_00108.text: MatPES‑trained UMLIPs produce lower fingerprint distances and comparable or slightly higher formation‑energy errors than MPRelax‑trained models, demonstrating superior structural‑relaxation accuracy.

clai_00109.text: TensorNet‑MatPES predicts ionic conductivities of Li/Na solid electrolytes with high fidelity (positive R²), whereas TensorNet‑MPF severely overestimates conductivities and yields a negative R².

clai_00110.text: The MatPES v2025.1 dataset contains 504,811 structures (434,712 PBE and 387,897 r2SCAN calculations) sampled from a configuration space of ~281 million MD snapshots and ~16 billion atomic environments.

clai_00111.text: The 2DIRECT sampling workflow yields a data‑efficient dataset that, despite being a fraction of the size of MPRelax, samples a substantially larger region of structural and atomic‑environment space.

clai_00112.text: The r2SCAN functional provides a more accurate description of interatomic bonding than PBE, leading to improved potential‑energy‑surface quality in the MatPES r2SCAN dataset.

clai_00113.text: Compared with MPRelax and OMat24, the MatPES PBE dataset exhibits a more Gaussian‑like distribution of cohesive energies per atom and a log‑normal‑like distribution of force magnitudes, indicating a better balance of on‑ and off‑equilibrium structures.

clai_00114.text: Training a TensorNet model on the 400 k‑structure MatPES‑PBE dataset requires approximately 15 minutes per epoch on a single RTX A6000 GPU, whereas training on the 100 M‑structure OMat24 dataset needs about 20 hours per epoch on sixteen A100 GPUs, highlighting the computational efficiency of MatPES.

clai_00115.text: TransIP achieves SO(3) equivariance through training with a contrastive latent equivariance objective rather than hard-wired equivariant architectural constraints.

clai_00116.text: A generic unconstrained Transformer can serve as an effective backbone for machine-learned interatomic potentials without explicit equivariance constraints.

clai_00117.text: TransIP achieves 40% to 60% improvement in performance compared to data augmentation baseline (TransAug) across varying OMol25 dataset sizes.

clai_00118.text: In the limited data regime (1M samples), TransIP achieves 255 meV/Å force MAE versus 600 meV/Å for TransAug, with force cosine similarity of 0.7 versus 0.44.

clai_00119.text: TransIP achieves 58 meV/atom energy MAE compared to TransAug's 120 meV/atom at 1M training samples.

clai_00120.text: TransIP-S and TransIP-M achieve significantly faster inference than eSEN baseline at 160,000 and 70,000 atoms/sec versus 15,000 atoms/sec respectively.

clai_00121.text: TransIP-L outperforms eSEN-sm in total energy prediction (1.60 vs 1.89 meV/atom MAE) and is competitive in total force MAE after 80 epochs of training.

clai_00122.text: TransIP attains comparable performance to state-of-the-art equivariant baselines (eSCN, GemNet-OC) on the OMol25 benchmark for machine-learning force fields.

clai_00123.text: Lower latent equivariance error is monotonically associated with better model performance across all evaluation metrics.

clai_00124.text: A 48% reduction in equivariance error from 1M to 4M training examples translates to 40-60% performance improvements, exceeding what would be expected from data scaling alone.

clai_00125.text: TransIP learns an embedding where input rotations act approximately as a shared orthogonal transformation across different molecules despite no explicit equivariance in the architecture.

clai_00126.text: Energy predictions show near-linear scaling with equivariance error, while force predictions exhibit two-regime behavior with disproportionate gains at higher data scales.

clai_00127.text: TransIP scales smoothly with parameter count while TransAug exhibits poorer scaling with larger models performing worse than smaller ones.

clai_00128.text: TransIP maintains performance advantages over TransAug across different molecular categories including biomolecules, electrolytes, metal complexes, and neutral organics.

clai_00129.text: TransIP uses a single-stage training pipeline without requiring separate pretraining-finetuning framework or explicit equivariance constraints.

clai_00130.text: The Message Passing Neural Network (MPNN) achieves state‑of‑the‑art performance on all QM9 regression targets, reaching chemical accuracy on 11 of the 13 targets and outperforming prior models such as SchNet and DTNN.

clai_00131.text: Inference with the MPNN takes roughly 10⁻² seconds per molecule, about 300,000 times faster than the DFT reference calculation (~10³ seconds).

clai_00132.text: The multiple‑tower architecture reduces the computational complexity of a propagation step from O(n²d²) to O(n²d²/k) and yields a 2× speedup for n=9, d=200, k=8.

clai_00133.text: A general training method allows MPNNs to use larger node representation dimensions without increasing computation time or memory, providing substantial savings over previous high‑dimensional MPNNs.

clai_00134.text: Introducing a virtual edge type for pairs of non‑connected nodes enables long‑distance information propagation during message passing.

clai_00135.text: Adding a latent master node that connects to every atom provides a global scratch space, allowing larger hidden dimensions with minimal performance penalty.

clai_00136.text: Using a pair‑message function that depends on both source and destination node states improves message‑passing efficiency compared with the standard matrix‑multiplication message function.

clai_00137.text: The Message Passing Neural Network framework unifies eight previously proposed graph‑based neural models under a single formalism.

clai_00138.text: Learning directly from molecular graphs without handcrafted descriptors enables the MPNN to achieve lower prediction errors than descriptor‑based methods.

clai_00139.text: Across all QM9 properties, the MPNN reduces the mean absolute error by 30–70 % relative to the best previously reported graph‑neural‑network baseline.

clai_00140.text: For internal energy at 0 K (U0), enthalpy (H), Gibbs free energy (G), heat capacity at constant volume (Cv), and highest vibrational frequency (Ω), the MPNN records lower mean absolute errors than SchNet and DTNN (U0 MAE 0.45 vs 0.55/0.72; H 0.39 vs 0.59/0.80; G 0.44 vs 0.55/0.74; Cv 0.80 vs 0.99/1.71; Ω 0.19 vs 0.41/0.78).

clai_00141.text: Standard Gaussian quadrature rules produce frame‑dependent (non‑objective) phase‑averaged internal energies for rotated crystal lattices.

clai_00142.text: Gaussian quadrature leads to abrupt energy jumps and fictitious minima when neighbor cut‑off radii change during large deformations.

clai_00143.text: Third‑order Gaussian quadrature fails to approximate phase‑space integrals for bulk aluminum above 300 K, producing spurious minima in the Helmholtz free‑energy landscape.

clai_00144.text: Fifth‑order Gaussian quadrature yields internal energies and free‑energy curves that remain in good agreement with molecular dynamics results across the full temperature range studied.

clai_00145.text: An E(3)‑equivariant graph neural network architecture guarantees rotational invariance of predicted phase‑averaged quantities.

clai_00146.text: The E(3)‑equivariant GNN surrogate provides superior accuracy compared with third‑ and fifth‑order Gaussian quadrature for thermal expansion of copper, martensitic phase transition of iron, and grain‑boundary energy calculations, matching molecular dynamics reference data.

clai_00147.text: The GNN surrogate achieves mean absolute errors of ≤0.313 meV for energy, ≤0.189 meV/Å for forces, and ≤0.0734 meV/Å² for thermal forces on validation sets.

clai_00148.text: Inference with the trained GNN is significantly faster than evaluating fifth‑order Gaussian quadrature, enabling frequent high‑dimensional integral evaluations and quasistatic finite‑temperature atomistic simulations without costly MD averaging.

clai_00149.text: Training the GNN on high‑fidelity Monte‑Carlo integration data enables accurate prediction of phase‑averaged energies and their derivatives for atomic clusters.

clai_00150.text: The GNN‑assisted integration framework can be applied to high‑dimensional integration problems beyond atomistics.

clai_00151.text: Incorporating E(3)‑equivariance into the GNN architecture provides a significant performance boost over standard multilayer perceptrons for phase‑space integration tasks.

clai_00152.text: DeePMD-kit is an open-source software package that facilitates molecular dynamics simulations using Deep Potential machine learning potentials for computational chemistry and materials science.

clai_00153.text: DeePMD-kit supports multiple atomic descriptor types including local frame, DeepPot-SE, attention-based, and hybrid descriptors.

clai_00154.text: The DeepPot-SE descriptor is continuous up to the second-order derivative in its domain, unlike the local frame descriptor which is not smooth at the cutoff radius and when exchanging the order of two nearest neighbors.

clai_00155.text: None of the tested descriptors outperforms the others in terms of accuracy across all datasets.

clai_00156.text: Type embedding reduces the number of neural network parameters and improves computing efficiency for systems with large numbers of chemical species by having all species share the same network parameters.

clai_00157.text: Compressed models are 1x-10x faster than the original models for both training and inference.

clai_00167.text: Long-range correction schemes in machine learning interatomic potentials are essential for achieving state-of-the-art accuracy, improving in-distribution performance, and enabling significant gains in transferability to unseen regions of chemical space.

clai_00174.text: Strictly local MLIP models overestimate short-range interactions to compensate for missing or incorrectly modeled long-range contributions.

clai_00175.text: Metal-organic frameworks present an ideal application for MLIPs because classical force fields lack required accuracy while DFT is too computationally expensive for large unit cells and long timescales.

clai_00176.text: Increasing the number of message passing steps can lead to overfitting and decreased performance compared to baseline models.

clai_00177.text: Total charge embeddings can recover much of CELLI's performance on some datasets but generalize poorly in size-based extrapolation and should be viewed as a potential extension rather than replacement for long-range methods.

clai_00178.text: The observed improvements from long-range corrections cannot be attributed to increased model capacity as all variants share identical hyperparameters and nearly identical parameter counts.

clai_00179.text: EFA and CELLI do not lead to improvements when no reference charges are provided in the ODAC25 dataset.

clai_00182.text: NequIP achieves state-of-the-art accuracy on the MD-17 benchmark, surpassing invariant GNN‑IPs, shallow neural networks, and kernel‑based methods.

clai_00183.text: NequIP outperforms kernel‑based approaches such as sGDML and FCHL19/GPR across benchmarks, including small-data regimes and the MD-17 dataset.

clai_00184.text: NequIP requires up to three orders of magnitude fewer training configurations than existing neural interatomic potentials to reach comparable accuracy.

clai_00185.text: When trained on only 133 structures (~1 k frames), NequIP outperforms DeepMD trained on 133,500 structures for liquid water and ice simulations.

clai_00186.text: Using higher-order E(3)-equivariant representations (increasing rotation order from l=0 to l=1 and up to l=3) consistently reduces prediction error and improves accuracy across all evaluated tasks.

clai_00187.text: Predicting forces as the negative gradient of the learned total energy guarantees energy conservation and rotation‑equivariant forces.

clai_00188.text: The equivariant architecture scales linearly with the number of atoms because convolutions are limited to a local cutoff radius.

clai_00189.text: NequIP attains chemical‑accuracy energy errors (~2 meV) on CCSD(T) benchmark molecules using only 1,000 reference configurations, outperforming sGDML and GemNet.

clai_00190.text: NequIP reproduces structural and kinetic properties from ab‑initio molecular dynamics simulations with high fidelity.

clai_00191.text: The universal HamGNN model achieves a mean absolute error of 5.4 meV for the real‑space Hamiltonian matrix on the test set after the first round of training.

clai_00192.text: Fine‑tuning the universal model on a small MOF dataset reduces the Hamiltonian matrix MAE to approximately 3.95 meV.

clai_00193.text: The universal HamGNN model accurately predicts the energy band structures and charge densities of complex multi‑element crystals (e.g., Hf2Zr9Ta6Ti5Nb5B54, HfTaTiB4MoC4, K3Ba3Li2Al4B6O20F), matching DFT results.

clai_00194.text: For the disordered solid‑electrolyte Li10Si1.5P1.5S11.5Cl0.5, the universal model predicts an insulating behavior with a band gap of 1.4 eV.

clai_00195.text: The universal HamGNN model accurately predicts the electronic structure of low‑dimensional systems, including a 1625‑atom MoS2/WS2 twisted bilayer (3.5°) and a C60 cluster, reproducing DFT band structures and HOMO wavefunctions.

clai_00196.text: High‑throughput screening of 188,722 GeNOME crystals with the universal model identifies 21,973 insulators (3,940 direct‑gap) and 5,109 flat‑band materials, nearly doubling the entries in the Materials Flatband Database.

clai_00197.text: Using the universal HamGNN model reduces computational cost by several orders of magnitude compared with DFT (e.g., 0.33 core·hours versus 181 core·hours for a large MOF) while preserving accuracy of band gaps and charge‑density differences.

clai_00198.text: A two‑step training procedure—first minimizing real‑space Hamiltonian error, then adding orbital‑energy error at random k‑points—is essential to obtain a truly universal Hamiltonian model.

clai_00199.text: Incorporating orbital‑energy loss in a second fine‑tuning round markedly improves band‑structure predictions, yielding energy bands and Fermi surfaces that closely match DFT calculations for the test set.

clai_00200.text: The universal HamGNN model generalizes to crystals containing more than five distinct elements and to any element supported by the OpenMX PBE pseudopotential library, effectively covering the entire periodic table.

clai_00201.text: xDeepH achieves sub‑meV mean absolute error on DFT Hamiltonian matrix elements for the test set of CrI3 configurations.

clai_00202.text: xDeepH accurately reproduces DFT band structures of (16,16) CrI3 nanotubes for both non‑collinear surface‑normal magnetization and collinear ferromagnetism.

clai_00203.text: xDeepH accurately predicts the band structure of monolayer NiBr2 with a 19×1×1 spin‑spiral magnetic order, matching DFT results.

clai_00204.text: xDeepH generalizes to Moiré‑twisted bilayer CrI3 at a twist angle of 81.79°, a configuration not seen during training, reproducing band structures and density of states in agreement with DFT.

clai_00205.text: xDeepH reduces the computational cost of electronic‑structure calculations relative to conventional constrained DFT, enabling simulations of magnetic superstructures containing thousands of atoms, such as a 4,336‑atom skyrmion supercell.

clai_00206.text: Embedding the full E(3) × {I, T} equivariance into the neural‑network architecture reduces the amount of training data required and improves prediction accuracy.

clai_00207.text: Introducing magnetic moments via a strictly localized magnetic‑moment layer yields more efficient and accurate training than treating atomic and magnetic structures on equal footing.

clai_00208.text: The DFT Hamiltonian H_DFT({R},{M}) obeys nearsightedness with two distinct length scales: RN2 ≈ R_C for magnetic‑structure influence and RN1 several times larger for atomic‑structure influence, as confirmed by numerical experiments.

clai_00209.text: The time‑reversal symmetry of the DFT Hamiltonian is enforced by assigning a parity index t to equivariant vectors, ensuring Hamiltonian sub‑blocks transform correctly under the anti‑unitary T operation.

clai_00210.text: The ENN architecture of xDeepH preserves equivariance under the Euclidean and time‑reversal symmetry group E(3)×{I,T}, which is essential for the method's performance.

clai_00211.text: The presence of a magnetic skyrmion in Moiré‑twisted CrI3 removes an extremely flat valence band that appears in the ferromagnetic configuration, indicating strong coupling between the flat band and the skyrmion.

clai_00212.text: The AFLOW standard enables reproducible high-throughput DFT calculations through standardized parameter sets for k-point density, energy cut-offs, exchange-correlation functionals, pseudopotentials, DFT+U parameters, and convergence criteria.

clai_00213.text: The AFLOWLIB repository contains calculated properties of over 625,000 materials across Binary Alloy Project, Electronic Structure database, Heusler database, and Elements database.

clai_00214.text: AFLOW calculations follow a standardized sequential workflow: RELAX1 → RELAX2 → STATIC → BANDS for materials in the Elements, ICSD, and Heusler databases.

clai_00215.text: Default NKPPRA values for non-BANDS calculations vary by database: Binary Alloy uses 6000 for RELAX, Heusler uses 10000 for STATIC and 6000 for RELAX, and ICSD uses 10000 for STATIC and 8000 for RELAX.

clai_00216.text: The PBE functional combined with PAW potentials is the default exchange-correlation functional and potential combination for ICSD, Binary Alloy, and Heusler databases.

clai_00217.text: The applied plane-wave kinetic energy cut-off (Ecut) is the largest recommended value among all species in the calculation, increased by a factor of 1.4.

clai_00218.text: DFT+U corrections are applied to the entire ICSD database and certain Heusler database entries containing O, S, Se, and F elements, but not to the Binary Alloy database.

clai_00219.text: Specific Ueff parameters are defined for d-block elements (Table 4) and U, J parameters for f-block elements (Table 5) to correct self-interaction error in DFT+U calculations, with values ranging from 1.9 eV (In) to 7.5 eV (Zn).

clai_00220.text: The first RELAX calculation is performed in collinear spin-polarized fashion with initial magnetic moments set to 1.0 µB per atom, and spin polarization is turned off in subsequent calculations if magnetization is below 0.025 µB/atom.

clai_00221.text: Electronic convergence criteria are δEelec = 10⁻⁵ eV and ionic convergence criteria are δEion = 10⁻⁴ eV for Elements database entries, while all other databases use δEelec = 10⁻³ eV and δEion = 10⁻² eV.

clai_00222.text: Following the AFLOW standard enables materials science researchers to reproduce AFLOWLIB consortium results and make direct comparisons of properties between different materials for identifying trends and formulating design rules.

clai_00223.text: BANDS calculations use 128 k-points per segment for single element structures and 20 k-points for compounds along high-symmetry paths.

clai_00224.text: The AFLOWLIB data is accessible through a REST-API for standardized data exchange.

clai_00225.text: The Gaussian Approximation Potential (GAP) for silicon reproduces density functional theory reference results across a wide range of observable properties, including bulk crystal, liquid, amorphous phases, and point, line, and plane defects.

clai_00226.text: For bulk elastic constants (B, C11, C12, C44) the GAP model achieves fractional errors of less than 10% relative to DFT, outperforming all other evaluated interatomic potentials.

clai_00227.text: Surface energies of the (111), (110) and (100) silicon cleavage planes are predicted by GAP with errors of around 2% relative to DFT, which is comparable or better than other potentials.

clai_00228.text: Formation energies of vacancy and interstitial point defects (hexagonal, tetrahedral, dumbbell) are predicted by GAP within 10% of DFT values, providing uniform accuracy across these defects.

clai_00229.text: For extrapolative planar defects not included in the training set—specifically the (112) Σ3 grain boundary and unstable stacking fault energies on the (111) shuffle and glide planes—GAP errors remain within 20% of DFT, outperforming other models.

clai_00230.text: Combining a simple repulsive pair potential with a many‑body SOAP‑kernel term in the GAP framework yields meV‑per‑atom accuracy for silicon energetics.

clai_00231.text: The Gaussian process regression framework underlying GAP provides an uncertainty quantification that qualitatively estimates the potential’s accuracy for any given atomic configuration.

clai_00232.text: Using the GAP model enables simulations that would be prohibitively expensive with DFT, such as finite‑temperature phase‑boundary calculations, liquid self‑diffusivity, amorphous silicon formation by slow quench, and dynamic brittle fracture.

clai_00233.text: A training database of manageable size, constructed from DFT configurations covering relevant phases and defects, is sufficient to achieve high transferability of the GAP model across diverse silicon configurations.

clai_00234.text: Benchmark comparisons show that the new GAP model yields lower errors than previous GAP models for silicon.

clai_00235.text: The Smooth Overlap of Atomic Positions (SOAP) kernel captures the regularity of the silicon potential energy surface, leading to accurate interpolation within the sampled configuration space.

clai_00236.text: MACE-MP-0 achieves the lowest mean absolute error (0.310 eV) in migration barrier predictions across the entire Dataset-2 of 574 migration paths.

clai_00237.text: Orb-v3 achieves the lowest MAE (0.198 eV) when evaluated on non-outlier data points (excluding systems with absolute errors >1 eV).

clai_00238.text: Orb-v3 and SevenNet classify materials as good versus bad ionic conductors with accuracy greater than 82% using a 500 meV migration barrier threshold.

clai_00239.text: All MLIPs struggle with high migration barrier predictions, with only 3.7-20.7% achieving acceptable accuracy (<0.1 eV error) in the 1.31-2.50 eV range.

clai_00240.text: There is no evident correlation between migration barrier prediction accuracy and local geometry prediction accuracy across all MLIPs.

clai_00241.text: SevenNet exhibits the highest fraction of good local geometry predictions (0.719) while MACE-MP-0 exhibits the lowest fraction of bad geometry predictions (0.190) among all tested MLIPs.

clai_00242.text: MACE-MP-0 and SevenNet intermediate images provide better initial guesses relative to conventional interpolation techniques in over 71% of structures.

clai_00243.text: MLIP-NEB relaxations produce intermediate image geometries closer to DFT-NEB references than linear interpolation in over 66% of structures.

clai_00244.text: M3GNet and CHGNet exhibit systematic bias toward underestimating migration barriers, with 73.1% and 78.2% of predictions being underestimates respectively.

clai_00245.text: For high migration barrier systems, MLIPs achieve their best geometry predictions but worst barrier predictions, indicating an inverse relationship.

clai_00246.text: CHGNet and M3GNet demonstrate superior performance for materials with low migration barriers but lack consistency over wider barrier ranges.

clai_00247.text: Orb-v3 exhibits the slowest degradation in prediction accuracy as migration barrier values increase compared to other MLIPs.

clai_00248.text: In the low-barrier range of 0.0025-0.25 eV, more than 50% of predictions achieve acceptable accuracy across all MLIPs tested.

clai_00249.text: IDPP interpolation does not make a significant difference in enhancing the initial guess for the minimum energy path compared to linear interpolation across all MLIPs.

clai_00250.text: Orb-v3 and SevenNet are suitable for high-throughput screening of candidate battery materials based on their >82% classification accuracy for ionic conductors.

clai_00251.text: FastCHGNet trains in 1.5 hours using 32 GPUs compared to 8.3 days on a single A100 GPU for the original CHGNet model.

clai_00252.text: MLIPs map atomic configurations to total energy and provide forces and stresses as analytical derivatives of the potential energy surface.

clai_00253.text: MLIPs use highly flexible functional forms (e.g., neural networks) while PBPs use highly constrained forms guided by physical intuition (e.g., Lennard-Jones).

clai_00279.text: MLIPs bridge the historical disconnect between AIMD (high accuracy, small scale) and PBP-based MD (larger scale, lower accuracy).

clai_00311.text: Matbench v0.1 is a benchmark suite containing 13 supervised machine learning tasks (10 regression, 3 classification) for materials property prediction, with dataset sizes ranging from 312 to 132,752 samples.

clai_00312.text: Matbench contains data from 10 density functional theory-derived and experimental sources including Materials Project, Zhuo et al., Landolt-Bornstein Handbook, Castelli et al., JARVIS DFT 2D, and Citrine Informatics.

clai_00313.text: Matbench tasks include predicting optical, thermal, electronic, thermodynamic, tensile, and elastic properties given materials composition and/or crystal structure.

clai_00314.text: Automatminer is a fully-automated machine learning pipeline consisting of four stages (autofeaturization, cleaning, dimensionality reduction, and AutoML search) that requires no user intervention or hyperparameter tuning.

clai_00315.text: Automatminer Express preset achieves the best performance on 8 of 13 tasks in the Matbench benchmark.

clai_00316.text: Automatminer's auto-generated models outperform or equal the Random Forest model across all Matbench tasks except predicting formation energies across the Materials Project.

clai_00317.text: Graph network models (CGCNN and MEGNet) have high errors on small datasets (<10^4 samples) but leverage large datasets more efficiently, outperforming traditional ML and AutoML approaches on tasks with approximately 10^4 data points or more.

clai_00318.text: Descriptor-based Automatminer and RF models have lower errors on small datasets but their improvement rates are shallower, with AutoML's advantage over conventional techniques narrowing as sample count increases and essentially lost near 10^5 samples.

clai_00319.text: All algorithms exhibit a universal trend of decreasing relative errors as dataset size increases.

clai_00320.text: For small datasets (<10^4 samples), inexpensive Automatminer presets (~1-5 minute training) retain the bulk of performance compared to expensive presets (24h+ training), with Express retaining 95% or more of the accuracy of more expensive presets at less than 50% of the computational cost on data-scarce tasks.

clai_00321.text: Graph networks (CGCNN and MEGNet) far outperform traditional ML algorithms on formation energy prediction tasks, with MEGNet decisively outperforming Automatminer for the PhDOS task; among nine structure-based tasks, Automatminer and MEGNet each achieve best scores on 4 tasks.

clai_00322.text: Matbench provides a consistent evaluation framework using five-fold nested cross-validation on identical folds across all algorithms to minimize comparison bias, with datasets pre-cleaned to remove unphysical computed data and task-irrelevant experimental data.

clai_00323.text: Automatminer source code and pre-processed Matbench tasks are open source and available online.

clai_00324.text: The frozen-framework PES descriptor screening ranks lithium-containing Materials Project compounds such that eight of the ten highest‑ranked materials are confirmed to be room‑temperature superionic conductors by first‑principles calculations.

clai_00325.text: The proposed screening method is approximately 50 × faster than molecular dynamics driven by a machine‑learning interatomic potential and at least 3 000 × faster than first‑principles molecular dynamics.

clai_00326.text: The combined descriptor Ξ, defined as the product of sigmoid‑transformed connected and disconnected free‑volume descriptors at a 0.5 eV threshold, achieves higher ranking scores than each individual descriptor and far exceeds random‑guess performance.

clai_00327.text: Free‑volume (FV) descriptors evaluated at energy thresholds between 0.3 eV and 0.5 eV consistently outperform or match the minimal percolation energy (MPE) descriptor across all three evaluation scores.

clai_00328.text: Using the frozen‑framework approximation, where only a single Li ion moves while the host lattice remains fixed, reduces the generalization error of the ML‑IAP compared with fully relaxed MD or NEB simulations.

clai_00329.text: AIMD simulations of the five top‑Ξ candidates confirm high ionic conductivities (e.g., Li(BH)6 shows σ ≈ 0.9 S cm⁻¹ at 1000 K with activation energy 219 ± 86 meV), validating the screening predictions.

clai_00330.text: The screening pipeline, when applied to 5 997 lithium‑containing Materials Project structures that satisfy basic stability and band‑gap criteria, yields 1302 structures after removing transition‑metal containing compounds, of which 113 have Ξ > 0.25.

clai_00331.text: The proposed descriptor‑based screening approach is not tied to a specific ML‑IAP; it can be employed with any universal interatomic potential model.

clai_00332.text: All evaluated descriptors (MPE, FV‑connected, FV‑disconnected) achieve ranking scores above those of a random‑guess classifier, demonstrating predictive capability for ionic conductivity.

clai_00333.text: Finite‑size tests using a larger supercell and an ML‑IAP (SevenNet) show that diffusion coefficients converge within statistical uncertainties, confirming that the AIMD results are not significantly affected by supercell size.

clai_00334.text: The Ξ descriptor screening increases the proportion of room‑temperature superionic candidates from ~7% in an unbiased sample to 55% in the top‑100 Ξ‑ranked list, an ~8‑fold improvement.

clai_00335.text: AIMD simulations of the ten highest‑ranking Ξ‑predicted materials show that eight of them are superionic at room temperature.

clai_00336.text: LiB3H8 exhibits an AIMD‑derived ionic conductivity of 82 ± 23 mS cm⁻¹ at 363 K, the highest among all screened candidates.

clai_00337.text: SevenNet‑driven MD ranks LiB3H8 as having the highest extrapolated room‑temperature conductivity, roughly an order of magnitude larger than the reference Li7P3S11.

clai_00338.text: Hydroborate structures appear at the top of the Ξ‑ordered list despite not being present in the training datasets, demonstrating the method’s generalization capability.

clai_00339.text: All AIMD‑tested structures are diffusive at 1000 K, and 88 % of the top‑100 Ξ‑selected materials are diffusive in the SevenNet‑driven MD validation.
